porbos.title: The Question From Which the Seerah Begins • The Love Even an Enemy Recognises • Uhud’s Shield, and the Price of Love • Love Is Not Born Without Knowing • This Love Is Not an Extra, It Is a Condition of Faith

blocks.0: The Question From Which the Seerah Begins
blocks.1: Dear reader, we have sat down to read about a man whom our eyes have never seen; and yet, fourteen hundred years on, in millions upon millions of hearts, love stirs the moment his name is mentioned, and a prayer of blessing (durood) upon him comes to the lips. But the first question of this book is not about him. The question is about me. About you.
blocks.2: The people of your home, the old customers at your shop, the stranger who sits beside you on the bus every morning: they watch you every day. Not your words, only your movements. How you get up, how you sit. What your face does when you are angry, what your eyes do when you laugh. How far your hand opens in a transaction, how soft your voice grows in speech. After watching for so long, do they ever sense that deep inside this person there is a profound attachment to someone? That this person loves someone dearly?
blocks.3: We all say, ‘I love the Prophet {{1}}.’ Saying it does not cost even a breath. We say it in gatherings, we sing it on the night of Milad, we say it with eyes wet when naming a child. If anyone voices even the slightest doubt, it is as though we catch fire at once. But however easily the claim comes to the lips, the proof does not come so easily. Love is a thing inside the chest. To bring it outside, to stand it up, to weigh it and show it to others, is no easy matter.
blocks.4: And yet, this very hard proof once opened itself, unasked, before one man. It was fourteen hundred years ago. The man was not a Muslim. He had not come to hear any talk about love. He had come as an envoy of the enemy side, to haggle over the terms of a treaty. For a while he sat quietly. He kept only his two eyes open. And in that short while something caught his notice that he could not help telling his own people when he returned to Makkah.
blocks.5: So let the first lesson of the Seerah begin through the eyes of that unfamiliar man.
blocks.6: The Love Even an Enemy Recognises
blocks.7: The plain of Hudaybiyyah. Bargaining over the terms of a treaty was under way. Several representatives of the Quraysh came to speak with the Prophet {{1}}. One of them was ‘Urwah ibn Mas‘ud, chief of the Thaqif tribe of Ta’if, an old ally of the Quraysh. Arab politics was as familiar to him as the lines of his own palm. Caesar, Chosroes, the Negus: he had seen every court.
blocks.8: He sat before the Prophet {{1}}. He spoke. He argued. And in between, his eyes swept around.
blocks.9: He saw the Prophet {{1}} making ablution, and the Companions not letting even a single drop of that water fall to the ground. As though, if one drop fell, something great would be lost. He saw that the moment the Prophet said a single word, everyone rushed to carry it out. Not one of them asked, even once, why. He saw that when the Prophet spoke, everyone’s voice before him dropped low of its own accord. No one could lift his eyes and keep looking at his face. Such respect, such love.
blocks.10: ‘Urwah stood up. Returning to Makkah, he said to the Quraysh—
blocks.11: “O Quraysh! I have been to the courts of kings. To Caesar, to Chosroes, to the Negus. By Allah, I have not seen any king whom his people honour as the companions of Muhammad honour Muhammad.”{{1}}
blocks.12: The man was not a Muslim. There was no need at all for him to say this. What would he gain by praising an enemy! Yet he said it. Because there was no way for this not to catch the eye.
blocks.13: ‘Urwah was not the only one to see this. It was a few years later. Zayd ibn al-Dathinna, a Companion captured in the Raji‘ expedition, had been brought to Makkah and taken out to be killed. Standing in the crowd was Abu Sufyan, who had not yet accepted Islam. He asked Zayd, “Don’t you wish that Muhammad were in your place today, and that you were sitting safe at home with your family?” Zayd answered—
blocks.14: “By Allah, I would not even like Muhammad {{1}} to have a thorn pricking his foot where he is now, in exchange for my sitting in my own home.”{{2}}
blocks.15: Abu Sufyan then said, “I have never seen anyone love another person as the companions of Muhammad love him.” This is the first sign of love. Love does not have to be announced aloud. It blooms of itself in the walking, in the glance, in the tone of the voice, in the care of the hands. And an outsider, a complete stranger, even an enemy, catches it in a single instant.
blocks.16: Uhud’s Shield, and the Price of Love
blocks.17: ‘Urwah saw it sitting in a quiet gathering. That day the sign of love was caught in good manners, in the tone of the voice, in the lowering of the eyes. But the true measure of love is taken elsewhere. Where a price has to be paid.
blocks.18: The field of Uhud. Arrows flying, the ranks broken, people scattered. The Prophet {{1}} was standing in the open field. A man came running. Talha ibn ‘Ubaydillah. An arrow was coming straight toward the Prophet {{2}}. Talha spread out his hand in front of the arrow. That very day the hand was finished. For the rest of his life that hand never moved again.
blocks.20: “I saw Talha’s hand paralysed. On the day of Uhud he shielded the Prophet {{1}} with this very hand.”{{2}}
blocks.21: One hand. Useless for a whole lifetime. In exchange, one arrow that did not touch the beloved. Is this a gain or a loss! What would Talha have said if asked!
blocks.22: There was another man on that field. Abu Talha (RA), the best archer of the Ansar. He took a shield and stood in front of the Prophet {{1}}. He held the shield not over himself but over him. That day two or three bows broke in his hands.
blocks.23: The Prophet {{1}} now and then wanted to raise his head to see the enemy’s position. And each time Abu Talha would tremble—
blocks.24: “May my father and mother be sacrificed for you! Do not raise your head, or some arrow of theirs will strike you. My chest is before your chest.”{{1}}
blocks.25: ‘My chest is before your chest.’ In this one sentence the entire lesson is held. The man is not calculating. He is not arguing. He is not setting conditions. He simply stands, making his body a wall; and he says, if an arrow must come, let it pass through my chest.
blocks.26: Not only on the field: this price of love was being paid in the homes of Madinah too. On the day of Uhud, word came to a woman of the Banu Dinar tribe that her father had been martyred. A little later, word came that her brother too. Then word came that her husband too. Each time she asked only one question: How is the Prophet {{1}}? People said, he is well. Still she was not at peace; she said, show me him once. Seeing the Prophet {{2}} safe and sound from afar, she said—
blocks.27: “As long as you are safe, every calamity is trivial.”{{1}}
blocks.28: What ‘Urwah had seen from the outside opened up from within at Uhud. What love is cannot be understood in the language of gatherings. It is understood at that moment when the price is asked.
blocks.29: Love Is Not Born Without Knowing
blocks.30: These people, who would not let the water of ablution fall to the ground: were they always like this? No.
blocks.31: ‘Umar ibn al-Khattab once set out with a drawn sword to finish off the Prophet {{1}}. Abu Sufyan came against him with an army three times over, at Badr, Uhud and the Trench. At Uhud the blood of Muslims flowed through Khalid’s tactics. ‘Ikrimah was the son of Abu Jahl. Wahshi’s spear pierced the chest of Hamzah (RA). And Hind chewed that liver. These very people. Exactly these became, later, the kind of people ‘Urwah had been speaking of.
blocks.32: How deep this change was can be sensed from a single remark of ‘Amr ibn al-‘As. The man who once rushed to the court of Abyssinia to bring the Companions back said, after accepting Islam—
blocks.33: “No one was dearer to me than the Messenger of Allah {{1}}, and no one was more majestic in my eyes. Out of reverence I could not even fill my eyes with looking at him. If anyone asks me to describe his appearance, I cannot; because I never looked at him with my eyes full.”{{2}}
blocks.34: No magic had happened in between. No spell had been recited. Only one thing had happened: suhbah, companionship. They came to know the man. And what a wonderful rule this is! Whoever has once truly come to know him has never been able to go back.
blocks.35: Here lies the real reason for reading the Seerah. Love cannot be built by scolding. By giving sermons, by shaming, by shouting ‘Love him, love him’; in no way at all. Love is born from just one thing: knowing. How can I love someone I do not know! And how can I help loving someone I have once truly come to know!
blocks.36: This Love Is Not an Extra, It Is a Condition of Faith
blocks.37: Someone might now think that this is merely an added beauty. Nice if you have it, fine if you do not. No, it is not fine. The Prophet {{1}} himself drew the line. He said—
blocks.39: “By the One in whose hand is my soul! None of you will be a believer until I am dearer to him than his father, his children and all of mankind.”{{1}}
blocks.40: This is worth pausing over. More than the father. More than the children. More than all people. A father’s love is the oldest love a person has. A child’s love is the deepest. One must pass beyond these two. And even then it is not the end.

footnotes.0: Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of Conditions, Chapter on the Conditions in Jihad and Reconciliation, hadith 2731–2732.
footnotes.1: Ibn Hisham, al-Sirah al-Nabawiyyah (the Raji‘ incident). A Seerah narration; it is not in the sound hadith collections.
footnotes.2: Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of Military Expeditions (al-Maghazi), Chapter on the Battle of Uhud, hadith 4063; on the authority of Qays ibn Abi Hazim (RH).
footnotes.3: Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of Military Expeditions, Chapter on the Battle of Uhud, hadith 4064; on the authority of Anas ibn Malik (RA).
footnotes.4: Ibn Hisham, al-Sirah al-Nabawiyyah (Uhud). A Seerah narration; it is not in the sound hadith collections.
footnotes.5: Sahih Muslim, Book of Faith, hadith 121.
footnotes.6: Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of Faith, Chapter: Love of the Messenger {{1}} Is Part of Faith, hadith 15; Sahih Muslim, Book of Faith, hadith 44; on the authority of Anas (RA).

quiz.q: According to Lesson 1, who is the first question of the book mainly about?
o: The reader and the author themselves
The Companions of the past, as is generally held
Only the Prophet ﷺ
Non-Muslim thinkers
quiz.e: The lesson says, ‘The first question of this book is not about him. The question is about me. About you.’

quiz.q: Of which tribe was ‘Urwah ibn Mas‘ud the chief at Hudaybiyyah?
o: The Quraysh of Makkah, as is generally held
The Thaqif of Ta’if
The Ghatafan of Najd
The Khazraj of Madinah
quiz.e: In the lesson’s words, ‘‘Urwah ibn Mas‘ud, chief of the Thaqif tribe of Ta’if, an old ally of the Quraysh.’

quiz.q: What behaviour of the Companions did ‘Urwah observe at Hudaybiyyah?
o: They were asking the reason behind the Prophet’s ﷺ commands
They were arguing among themselves over the terms of the treaty
They would not let even a drop of the ablution water fall to the ground
They were preparing their weapons and gear for war
quiz.e: ‘Urwah saw that the Companions ‘did not let even a single drop of that water fall to the ground’, that at a single word everyone rushed to act, and that before the Prophet ﷺ everyone’s voices dropped low.

quiz.q: What did ‘Urwah say to the Quraysh after returning to Makkah?
o: The Companions will never agree to a treaty
Caesar’s subjects obey him more
The Companions obey the Prophet ﷺ only out of fear
People do not honour any king like this
quiz.e: ‘Urwah said that although he had seen the courts of Caesar, Chosroes and the Negus, he had seen no king ‘whom his people honour as the companions of Muhammad honour Muhammad.’

quiz.q: In answer to Abu Sufyan’s question while in captivity, what did Zayd ibn al-Dathinna (RA) say?
o: He did not want even a thorn to prick the Prophet’s ﷺ foot
He would agree to a treaty in exchange for his release
He agreed to be in the Prophet’s ﷺ place
He agreed to return safely to his family at home
quiz.e: Hearing this answer, Abu Sufyan, then a non-Muslim, exclaimed, ‘I have never seen anyone love another as the companions of Muhammad love him.’

quiz.q: ‘Urwah, though not a Muslim, praised the Companions’ love before the Quraysh. What is the significance of this in the lesson?
o: He had secretly accepted Islam
It was so clear that even an enemy’s eye could not miss it
He said it as a diplomatic move
His main aim was to frighten the Quraysh
quiz.e: ‘Urwah had nothing to gain by praising an enemy; ‘yet he said it, because there was no way for this not to catch the eye’. Love shows itself in behaviour.

quiz.q: What became of the hand of Talha ibn ‘Ubaydillah (RA) on the day of Uhud?
o: The hand was cut off
The hand became paralysed that very day
The hand received only a slight scratch
The hand received a deep sword wound
quiz.e: He spread out his hand in front of the arrow coming toward the Prophet ﷺ; ‘that very day the hand was finished. For the rest of his life that hand never moved again.’

quiz.q: ‘My chest is before your chest.’ Who was standing with a shield on the field of Uhud saying this?
o: Talha ibn ‘Ubaydillah (RA)
Qays ibn Abi Hazim (RH)
Abu Talha al-Ansari (RA)
Anas ibn Malik (RA)
quiz.e: Abu Talha (RA), ‘the best archer of the Ansar’, was shielding the Prophet ﷺ with a shield, and said this each time the Prophet raised his head.

quiz.q: What do ‘Urwah’s testimony and the events of Uhud, taken together, show about love?
o: Both speak only of the manners of gatherings, as is generally held
Love is proved only on the battlefield
In a gathering it shows in good manners; at Uhud, in paying the price
Love is not really something to be proved
quiz.e: ‘Urwah saw it in a quiet gathering, ‘in good manners, in the tone of the voice, in the lowering of the eyes’; but the true measure is taken ‘where a price has to be paid’.

quiz.q: What is the story of the woman of Banu Dinar on the day of Uhud brought in the lesson to show?
o: That women too took part on the battlefield then
That news cannot be believed without verification
That it is better not to show grief even when grieved
That the price of love was being paid in homes as well
quiz.e: In the lesson’s words, ‘Not only on the field: this price of love was being paid in the homes of Madinah too’. The woman said, ‘As long as you are safe, every calamity is trivial.’

quiz.q: ‘My chest is before your chest.’ Why does the lesson say that the ‘entire lesson’ is held in this one sentence?
o: It is a picture of shielding him with one’s life, without calculation
It reveals the whole military strategy of Uhud, as is generally held
It is the name of a famous hadith book
It hints at the terms of the treaty
quiz.e: In the lesson’s words, ‘The man is not calculating. He is not arguing. He is not setting conditions’; he only makes his body a wall and says, if an arrow must come, let it pass through my chest.

quiz.q: According to the lesson, what was the ‘one thing only’ behind the transformation of the former enemies?
o: Long and strict training
Victories in one battle after another
Fear of harsh rule and punishment
Suhbah, that is, coming to know him
quiz.e: In the lesson’s words, ‘No magic had happened in between. No spell had been recited. Only one thing had happened: suhbah. They came to know the man.’

quiz.q: After accepting Islam, what would ‘Amr ibn al-‘As (RA) say about the Prophet ﷺ?
o: Out of reverence he could not lift his eyes to him
He would write down every word of the Prophet ﷺ
He had fought the Prophet ﷺ more than anyone
He could see the Prophet ﷺ only from afar
quiz.e: In the narration of Sahih Muslim, ‘Amr (RA) says, ‘No one was dearer to me than the Messenger of Allah ﷺ… Out of reverence I could not even fill my eyes with looking at him.’

quiz.q: ‘How can I love someone I do not know!’ What argument does the lesson build with these words?
o: Love is created only through sermons and scolding
Love comes from knowing, hence the reading of the Seerah
The Seerah is a subject written only for scholars
Love comes by inheritance from lineage
quiz.e: In the lesson’s words, ‘Love cannot be built by scolding… Love is born from just one thing: knowing.’ The Seerah is the path to that knowing.

quiz.q: Someone wants to create love of the Prophet ﷺ in others’ hearts by scolding and shaming. According to the lesson, what is wrong with this?
o: Love comes down through generations, not through effort
This is the most effective way of creating love
Instead of scolding, giving rewards alone will do
Love does not come this way; it comes from knowing
quiz.e: In the lesson’s words, ‘Love cannot be built by scolding… Love is born from just one thing: knowing’, which is why reading the Seerah is needed.

quiz.q: According to the hadith of the Prophet ﷺ, no one can be a believer until he is dearer to that person than…
o: his wealth, his clan and his friends
his father, his children and everyone else
his teacher, his friend and his relatives
his neighbour and his colleague
quiz.e: In the words of the hadith, ‘None of you will be a believer until I am dearer to him than his father, his children and all of mankind.’

quiz.q: Even after passing beyond the love of father and children, where does the measure of love end up?
o: The test of love takes place only in gatherings
Love is complete with the declaration of the mouth alone
The measure rises higher still and lands on one’s life
It is enough for love to be greater than wealth
quiz.e: The lesson says that after passing beyond father and children it is ‘not the end’; in the story of ‘Umar (RA) the measure becomes more than one’s own life.
